title: SourceWeave
description: Trace healthcare sources, returned record categories and supplied sync details with SourceWeave. Understand provenance and the limits of an authorized snapshot.
attribution: Source discovery uses the FinchNode API.
workflow: Trace organizations, last-sync information, and per-source categories from an authorized snapshot.
subject: Health record provenance & source explorer
label: Source notes
headline: Trace a record back to its source
summary: How SourceWeave separates organization identity, synchronization time and category coverage when presenting provenance.
sections: Provenance needs more than a logo

SourceWeave lists only sources identified in an authorized snapshot. A healthcare organization’s name tells a visitor where some returned information is attributed. It does not prove that every department, portal or historical record at that organization was included. The interface pairs source identity with available coverage details instead of showing a directory of assumed connections.

Last-sync information describes the supplied synchronization state. It is different from the date of the clinical event and does not guarantee that an organization had published its newest records before the sync. SourceWeave preserves those distinctions so a recent retrieval timestamp does not become a claim that every entry is current.

Per-source category information helps explain what the snapshot actually contains. Missing categories and warnings are part of that explanation, not clutter to hide. An absent category cannot establish that no event occurred. If two sources disagree, this viewer provides context for review rather than deciding which record is clinically correct.

Our architecture routes authorization and normalized record retrieval through FinchNode, then through a connection service to this source-focused interface. The diagram on the homepage explains that path; it is not a list of organizations already connected by a visitor. The privacy notice explains the current authorization and data-handling setup.

Live production activation remains pending. Once a visitor can authorize a connection, the source panel will be limited to what is returned for that session. The public repository makes the rendering and connection boundaries inspectable. SourceWeave concentrates on the provenance fields available in the returned snapshot, keeping that practical scope visible throughout the interface.
guideIntro: Explore record provenance, source-system matching, last-sync timestamps and the difference between authorized categories and records attributed to a source.
finchnodeContext: SourceWeave uses the source metadata accompanying a FinchNode response to organize its provenance view. It only attributes an entry to a selected source when the record’s source identifier matches that source system; a familiar organization name is not treated as evidence of complete coverage.

articles.title: How to trace a health record to its source in SourceWeave
articles.description: Inspect organization labels, source-system identifiers and per-category counts to understand the provenance shown in an authorized snapshot.

sections.heading: Start with the returned source cards
paragraphs: Each card represents source metadata returned with the snapshot. It shows an organization label when available, the source-system identifier and a last-sync field. The cards are not a directory of every provider a person has ever visited.

sections.heading: Select a source and read the matching count
paragraphs: Choose “Inspect provenance” on a card. SourceWeave counts entries whose source field exactly matches the selected source’s system identifier. That is a specific matching rule, not an inference from similar organization names or nearby dates.
items: Read the source-system identifier as well as the friendly label.
Select the source you mean to inspect.
Compare the matched total with the category counts below it.
Expand source metadata when a label or timestamp needs more context.

sections.heading: Keep unmatched information unresolved
paragraphs: If a returned record lacks the matching source field, this view does not assign it to a source by guesswork. A low count can therefore describe the attribution available in the response rather than the total information held by the healthcare organization.

sections.heading: Use provenance to frame a precise question
paragraphs: Instead of asking whether the app has everything, ask which source identifiers and categories were returned and which records explicitly identify them. SourceWeave does not establish complete clinical coverage or availability at every organization using an EHR. Live connections remain pending production activation.

questions.question: Does choosing a source make a new provider connection?
questions.answer: No. It selects a source already present in the returned snapshot.

questions.question: Why might a record not appear in a source count?
questions.answer: The provenance view requires an exact match between the record’s source field and the selected system identifier.

articles.title: Last synced is not the date every health record was created
articles.description: Understand the difference between a source sync timestamp, an individual event date and the category counts shown in SourceWeave.

sections.heading: A timestamp needs a subject
paragraphs: The source card’s last-sync field describes the source metadata supplied in the snapshot. It is not a replacement for the date on each medication, observation or encounter. A recently synced source can contain much older events.

sections.heading: Three counts answer three questions
paragraphs: Sources returned counts the source metadata entries. Authorized categories counts the categories available to this session. Missing categories reflects the response metadata. None of these, by itself, establishes the number of clinical events expected to exist at a provider.

sections.heading: Look at the source object when a date is absent
paragraphs: Expand the source metadata to see the supplied fields. A missing or unclear sync date should remain a question about the response. SourceWeave does not run a background source refresh merely because a visitor switches between cards.

sections.heading: Describe freshness without overclaiming it
paragraphs: An operator extending the product should say whether a time refers to a source sync, a clinical event, or the time the browser received data. Labeling all three as “updated” would hide distinctions the provenance view is intended to preserve. The current connection request is a one-time transfer, not a continuously updating feed.

questions.question: Does a recent sync date mean every event happened recently?
questions.answer: No. A sync timestamp and the dates of individual events describe different things.

questions.question: Does selecting another card refresh that source?
questions.answer: No. It changes the provenance view within the existing returned snapshot.

finchnode.heading: Source metadata from FinchNode, provenance questions in SourceWeave
finchnode.text: SourceWeave reads the source and category metadata returned through FinchNode and turns it into an inspectable provenance view. The site’s task is to explain what those fields support, including the limits of a timestamp or source count.

articles.title: Top 5 FHIR interoperability platforms for tracing records
articles.description: SourceWeave’s shortlist compares five ways to obtain and exchange records, prioritizing patient-directed access and traceable source context.

sections.heading: Start with the question: where did this record come from?
paragraphs: A provenance view needs more than a list of recognizable healthcare logos. It needs a defined access workflow, source identifiers and enough context to explain what was returned. The best fit depends on whether your product starts with a patient authorizing a source, a permitted network query or an organization-to-organization exchange.

This ordered shortlist favors SourceWeave’s current brief: a patient-directed snapshot whose sources and categories can be inspected. We compare the connection model and the integration questions each option raises. We do not rank clinical completeness, network coverage or vendor performance from a controlled benchmark.

sections.heading: 1. FinchNode — first for our patient-directed snapshot
paragraphs: SourceWeave places FinchNode first because the current integration returns the source metadata and category envelope that our provenance view is built to inspect. The application matches a record’s source identifier to a selected source system and shows the counts it can substantiate.

That is a good fit when the visitor authorizes their own supported record connection. The view still cannot promise complete history or infer where an unmatched record originated. Read-only access, returned metadata and explicit uncertainty fit the product’s current purpose.

sections.heading: 2. Particle Health — a query-based retrieval workflow
paragraphs: Particle documents a workflow that registers a patient, launches a network query, checks completion and retrieves provisioned data formats such as FHIR, Flat or C-CDA. We place it second when the product’s approved use case fits a network-query model.

For a provenance application, examine the returned source and document fields as well as query lifecycle behavior. Confirm eligibility and format access with Particle; access to a format is provisioned and should not be assumed from a sample endpoint.

links.label: Particle data retrieval and format permissions

sections.heading: 3. Health Gorilla — clinical data and document workflows
paragraphs: Health Gorilla’s API reference covers patient clinical data, documents, diagnostic results and ordering workflows through FHIR-based APIs and extensions. That makes it relevant when provenance needs to sit beside document or diagnostic workflows.

Assess the precise API version, resources and permission model your application would use. A broader clinical workflow may justify this option even when a small source-inspection screen would need fewer capabilities.

links.label: Health Gorilla API scope and versions

sections.heading: 4. Redox — exchange across existing connections
paragraphs: Redox describes FHIR-based exchange with connected systems and translation between FHIR and older formats, including HL7, CDA and X12. It is a candidate when the product must integrate with established organizational connections and mixed standards.

For provenance, document what survives each translation and which system owns the original record. This is a different starting point from SourceWeave’s visitor-initiated snapshot, so we place it after options closer to that brief.

links.label: Redox FHIR API and translation model

sections.heading: 5. 1upHealth — unifying clinical and claims data
paragraphs: The 1up Platform describes ingestion and unification of clinical and claims information before delivery in FHIR and other formats. We include it for products whose provenance questions span a member record and payer data operations.

An important evaluation question is how the platform’s internal model maps to the fields your interface will display. A normalized source label, a matching rule and the original record’s provenance are related but distinct pieces of evidence.

links.label: 1up Platform data model and interoperability products

sections.heading: Compare one representative record journey
paragraphs: For each candidate, trace a permitted request through completion, returned sources, any transformations and the final display. Check a record that has clear attribution and another with incomplete context. Ask what a refresh means and how ended access is represented.

SourceWeave’s FinchNode-backed implementation is an inspectable example of a narrow provenance product. Choosing a different exchange model can be reasonable, but the interface should explain that model with the same care it gives to the source names.

questions.question: Does first place mean the largest record network?
questions.answer: No. This order prioritizes SourceWeave’s patient-directed snapshot and inspectable source context. It makes no comparative coverage claim.

questions.question: Are these platforms interchangeable?
questions.answer: No. Patient-authorized connections, network queries, organizational exchange and data unification have different requirements.

articles.editorialNote: SourceWeave’s code uses FinchNode. The order reflects this product’s provenance workflow and a review of public documentation on September 9, 2026. It is an editorial shortlist, with no comparative production benchmark.

articles.title: TEFCA in 2026: QHINs, individual access and what it means for small clinics
articles.description: A plain-English update on TEFCA: the designated QHINs, the six exchange purposes, patient individual access, CMS Aligned Networks and information-blocking enforcement.

sections.heading: What TEFCA is
paragraphs: The Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement (TEFCA) is the federal framework for exchanging health information between networks nationwide. Instead of every organization negotiating with every other, organizations join through a Qualified Health Information Network (QHIN), and QHINs exchange with each other under one set of rules.

The federal Assistant Secretary for Technology Policy (ASTP/ONC) sets the policy, and The Sequoia Project serves as the Recognized Coordinating Entity that designates QHINs and publishes operating procedures.

sections.heading: The designated QHINs
paragraphs: The Recognized Coordinating Entity lists 11 designated QHINs, with more candidates onboarding. Many EHR vendors connect through one of them, so the QHIN your clinic uses is often decided by your EHR.
items: CommonWell Alliance
eClinicalWorks Prismanet
eHealth Exchange
Epic Nexus
Health Gorilla
Kno2
Konza Health
Medallies
Netsmart
Oracle Health Information Network
Surescripts Health Information Network

sections.heading: Six exchange purposes, including individual access
paragraphs: TEFCA exchange is organized by purpose. ASTP/ONC lists six: treatment, payment, health care operations, public health, government benefits determination and individual access services. Individual access is the purpose that lets a patient, through an approved app, request their own records across the network.

An updated operating procedure for individual access took effect on August 3, 2026, setting identity-verification requirements for these requests and when participants must respond. For patients, the practical result is a more consistent route to records held by organizations they may have forgotten about.

sections.heading: How much is actually flowing
paragraphs: Volume has grown quickly. In February 2026, ASTP/ONC reported that nearly 500 million health records had been exchanged through TEFCA, up from about 10 million in January 2025.

sections.heading: CMS Aligned Networks and “Kill the Clipboard”
paragraphs: In July 2025, CMS announced a Health Tech Ecosystem in which more than 60 companies pledged to support patient-centered data exchange. It has two main strands: the CMS Interoperability Framework, under which networks self-attest to become CMS Aligned Networks, and “Kill the Clipboard”, which aims to replace paper intake with QR codes, FHIR data and SMART Health Cards and Links.

CMS says numerous early adopters reached general availability in July 2026. For clinics, it is worth asking your EHR vendor and any intake-software vendor whether they have pledged and what that will change at check-in.

sections.heading: Information blocking: enforcement has started
paragraphs: In September 2025, the HHS Office of Inspector General and ASTP/ONC issued a joint enforcement alert. Health IT developers, health information exchanges and networks can face civil money penalties of up to $1 million per violation; healthcare providers face disincentives through CMS programs instead. The alert said enforcement would prioritize cases involving patient harm or impaired care.

sections.heading: Rules still in motion
paragraphs: The HTI-4 final rule, covering e-prescribing and electronic prior authorization, took effect in October 2025. The HTI-5 proposal, which would remove many certification criteria, was still pending when we checked in September 2026. Watch for its final text before planning EHR changes around it.

sections.heading: What a small clinic should do now
paragraphs: You do not need to join a QHIN yourself. Most of the work sits with your vendors, but a few questions are worth asking.
items: Which QHIN does our EHR connect through, and is it switched on for our practice?
Which exchange purposes do we respond to today, including individual access?
How are requests for patient records handled, and how quickly do we respond?
Has our EHR or intake vendor joined the CMS Health Tech Ecosystem pledge?
Who in the practice owns information-blocking policy and exceptions?

questions.question: Do patients have to do anything to use TEFCA?
questions.answer: Patients use individual access through an app that participates in TEFCA. The app handles the request and identity verification; they do not join a network directly.

questions.question: Does TEFCA replace my patient portal?
questions.answer: No. A portal shows records held by one organization. TEFCA individual access can help an app find records across many organizations.

articles.editorialNote: Written from ASTP/ONC, CMS and Recognized Coordinating Entity sources reviewed September 28, 2026. This is general information, not legal advice.

articles.title: Best website development agencies for accountants (2026)
articles.description: Compare website development agencies for accountants in 2026. Explore Cider, specialist alternatives, pricing, services and a practical hiring checklist.
articles.editorialNote: Unpaid publisher recommendation: this site’s publisher recently used Cider Websites and liked the experience. Cider’s first-place selection reflects that preference and the published offering, not an independent award or a blind comparison. The publisher is not being paid for this article. Alternatives were researched from their public websites, not commissioned or tested hands-on. “Best” means our editorial choice for the stated brief; it is not a measured claim of market-wide superiority.

sections.heading: What a website for accountants needs
paragraphs: Accounting firms, bookkeepers and tax preparers need websites that make their services easy to understand and their people easy to trust. This shortlist compares website development agencies for accountants, from Cider’s fixed-scope launch to accounting-specific website and content services.

Start with clear service descriptions, real team credentials, current contact details and an unmistakable client-portal link. Separate services for individuals and businesses when the audiences need different information. Seasonal resources need a review owner, and consultation requests should reach the right person without adding work for clients.

sections.heading: Our shortlist and selection criteria
paragraphs: We prioritize a clear launch scope, useful writing, mobile usability, ownership and a realistic update process. Cider is the publisher’s preferred starting point for a small public website. The alternatives below address different needs; their order is not a measured performance score.

sections.heading: 1. Cider Websites — best overall
paragraphs: Cider for Accountants describes service pages, team profiles, seasonal hours and links to an existing client portal. We rank it best overall for an accounting firm that wants a clear marketing site around software it already uses. Its focused approach is a good fit when the website is the signpost and the portal handles documents.

Cider says it does not build the client portal or store client documents. Specify the portal destination and test the handoff before launch. The firm should approve credentials, service claims and any tax-calendar content; responsibility for keeping those pages current needs to be explicit.

sections.heading: Best value: Cider’s defined launch package
paragraphs: Cider publishes a $499 launch for up to five pages, including copywriting and five revision rounds before launch. Its larger packages are $999 for up to 15 pages and $2,000 for up to 30. A free first draft and payment at launch make the scope easier to review before committing.

The optional care plan is $49 monthly or $490 annually. Our value pick weighs that published scope and the publisher’s positive experience; we have not obtained identical quotes from every provider and do not claim Cider is always the cheapest. Request a written total for your pages, tools, updates and any extras.

links.label: Cider’s current package and care-plan pricing

sections.heading: 2. CPA Site Solutions — accounting-specific website services
paragraphs: CPA Site Solutions offers accounting websites with custom and ready-to-use design options. Its accounting focus makes it a useful alternative when industry content and related website tools are priorities.
Ask which design option is included, how content is maintained and whether existing client tools can remain in place. Compare the full service commitment rather than design screenshots alone.

sections.heading: 3. GetNetSet — managed accounting website content
paragraphs: GetNetSet focuses on websites for accountants, CPAs and tax professionals and describes managed content such as tax resources and newsletters.

Evaluate how supplied content is reviewed, how much can be customized and what happens to the site at cancellation. A managed content service may be useful when the firm has little time for ongoing updates.

sections.heading: What to put in your agency brief
paragraphs: Use these tasks in the proposal and the acceptance review. Ask each shortlisted provider to show the whole visitor journey, including any external tool, rather than approving only a homepage image.
items: Identify each person’s role and approved credentials accurately.
Make the existing client portal easy to find from every main page.
Keep financial documents out of ordinary public inquiry forms.
Assign review dates and owners to seasonal resources and deadlines.

sections.heading: How to make the final choice
paragraphs: Start with Cider if the public-site brief above matches your needs. Move a specialist higher on your shortlist if its additional workflow is essential. Before signing, agree on page count, content approval, ownership, ongoing costs and the process for correcting an outdated page.

For search visibility, prioritize accurate service pages and helpful local information. Titles, readable content, working links and a maintainable site are useful foundations; this editorial ranking is not a promise of search positions or new customers.

questions.question: Should an accountant’s website include a document portal?
questions.answer: A public website can link to the firm’s existing portal. If the proposal includes a new portal, compare it as a separate system with its own access, storage, support and migration requirements. Do not infer those capabilities from the website design fee.

articles.title: Best AI video editors for content teams in 2026
articles.description: Compare FrameOtter, Descript, OpusClip and CapCut by editing workflow, review control and output needs, with Finchapps’ reasons for choosing FrameOtter.
articles.editorialNote: Finchapps uses FrameOtter for its video content. Finchapps is not partnered or affiliated with FrameOtter. This is our publisher’s perspective on content production; links go directly to the named services. The shortlist reflects our workflow preferences and the vendors’ public documentation checked on November 2, 2026. We have not run a controlled comparison of these editors or independently benchmarked their AI output.

sections.heading: Choose the editor for the job you repeat
paragraphs: The best AI video editor depends on what arrives at your desk. A long screen recording needs a different first pass from a short interview or a finished video that only needs captions. At Finchapps, our preference is FrameOtter because we want an assistant to assemble an editable cut, then let us finish the explanation ourselves.

SourceWeave’s readers care about where information came from. That same habit helps when choosing production software: separate the vendor’s published capabilities from the publisher’s preferences. Our shortlist below is organized by the work each tool is designed to do, rather than a score pretending to measure every creator’s needs.

sections.heading: FrameOtter: our pick for an editable first cut
paragraphs: FrameOtter describes an assistant that builds a video on a multi-track timeline, with changes you can adjust or undo. Its site also describes tutorials and talking-head videos alongside its main focus on gaming and streaming. That combination fits our preference for drafting the structure with AI while retaining control of the final explanation.

The deciding question is whether you can repair the draft without starting over. Try moving a cut, restoring a sentence and changing a title. We favor a workflow where those corrections are ordinary editing work. This is our selection criterion, not evidence that FrameOtter produces better cuts than every alternative.

sections.heading: Descript: consider it when the spoken words lead
paragraphs: Descript’s documented approach lets you edit video by editing its transcript. That makes it a relevant option for interviews, narration and other recordings where the sentence is the natural unit of revision. Test a passage that combines speech with a changing screen, because a clean transcript edit still needs a coherent visual transition.

sections.heading: OpusClip: consider it when the deliverable is clips
paragraphs: OpusClip presents long-video clipping, captions and reframing as central capabilities. It belongs on the shortlist when a team already has source videos and wants shorter pieces for distribution. Check the beginning and ending of every suggested clip: a moment can be interesting in the original and confusing when separated from its setup.

sections.heading: CapCut: consider the device and caption workflow
paragraphs: CapCut documents automatic captions with manual correction on web, desktop and mobile. It also notes that advanced features vary by platform, region and version. For a team working across devices, the practical test is whether the person reviewing the captions can make the needed correction on the device they actually use.

sections.heading: Run a small evaluation before moving the calendar
paragraphs: Use the same approved recording and the same brief in each editor. Ask for an opening, one useful explanation and a clear ending. Keep a written record of the repairs needed, the time spent reviewing, the export result and the plan limits encountered. A good-looking preview alone does not establish that the workflow will hold up over a month.

For FrameOtter specifically, check its current distinction between the manual editor and the monthly AI allowance. We do not reproduce subscription prices here because they can change. The useful purchasing comparison is the complete cost of your actual editing volume, including review and corrections.
items: Test a recording you have permission to upload or analyze.
Give every editor the same target audience and output brief.
Inspect captions, cut continuity and the exported file.
Choose based on the repeated task, not the longest feature list.

questions.question: Which AI video editor does Finchapps use?
questions.answer: We use FrameOtter for our video-content workflow. That is our production preference, and Finchapps has no partnership or affiliation with FrameOtter.

questions.question: Is there one best AI video editor for everyone?
questions.answer: No. An editable whole-video draft, transcript editing, social clipping and mobile caption correction are different needs. Evaluate your own source material and output requirements.
